title: Running a Chess YouTube Channel entirely by AI — Stephan Steinfurt, TNG

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is the agent architecture combining chess engines with LLMs via specialized tools for position analysis and video generation. The system produces creative media content for YouTube while demonstrating general-purpose agent architecture patterns. The system is deployed in production, running daily automated video generation for a live YouTube channel. The talk covers agent tool design and architecture concepts accessible to practitioners familiar with LLM agents. The video is a conference-style presentation with demo and Q&A. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct quotes from the talk.

summary: Stephan Steinfurt (TNG, based in Munich) presents an automated pipeline that creates daily chess puzzle explanation videos for YouTube entirely via AI. The project was highlighted in a major German newspaper as pursuing the 'holy grail of chess programming' — AI that explains chess as well as a human trainer. The fundamental problem is that traditional chess engines play well but cannot explain, while LLMs can describe but cannot play chess well; the solution combines both via an agent architecture. The pipeline downloads games from lichess nightly, analyzes them, and lets an agent with specialized tools produce explanations covering brilliant moves, blunders, and variations. The agent runs on Gemini 2.5 Pro, which Steinfurt calls the best model he has seen on chess, likely due to post-training. Tools include: a legal-moves checker to prevent hallucinated illegal moves; a virtual chessboard allowing the agent to play and retract moves to explore variations; a chess engine for evaluation; a checks-captures-threats tool providing beginner-relevant candidate moves beyond just the best move; and web search for historical context. The checks-captures-threats tool is emphasized as providing diversity, enabling the agent to explain human-reasonable moves, not just engine-optimal ones. The Maya engine from the University of Toronto, which can simulate moves at a given player rating, is referenced as a way to potentially target content for different skill levels. The evolution from Python-scripted analysis to reasoning-model-driven analysis is discussed; earlier Grok 4 was best, now Gemini 2.5 Pro is preferred. The agent itself decides which squares to highlight, which arrows to draw, and what constitutes a brilliant move. Video production uses ElevenLabs V3 for TTS with audio emotion tags. The channel has roughly 500k views and over 4,000 subscribers, most gained in the past month. It is not yet monetized and operates at a net loss. Average cost per video is 20-30 cents for short videos, but can reach euros for longer content. Cost optimization is not currently a priority; the team prefers erring on the side of better descriptions, though redundant tool calls and the agent replaying games twice are noted as optimization opportunities. The speaker has shifted to a more relaxed stance on errors, willing to take problematic videos down afterwards rather than manually reviewing every one. There is ongoing uncertainty about which difficulty level to target — some checkmate-in-one puzzles are trivial for strong players but valuable for absolute beginners. No other games have been explored yet, though extension is considered possible. Error rate is approximately 1 in 20 videos having notable issues such as a missed checkmate description.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Holy Grail Motivation
sections.summary: Steinfurt references a German newspaper article calling AI chess explanation the 'holy grail of chess programming,' noting it could take 5 years, but TNG in Munich is already producing fully AI-generated videos.

sections.title: Demo Video: Knight Fork Puzzle
sections.summary: A 2-minute AI-generated video is shown explaining a rook sacrifice on H5 leading to a knight-to-F6 fork that simultaneously attacks the king and queen on G4 or H5, demonstrating accessible tactical narration.

sections.title: Pipeline Overview
sections.summary: Videos are created nightly by downloading lichess games, analyzing them, running an agent for deeper analysis, producing a special format, and generating videos showing variations, brilliant moves, and blunders.

sections.title: Core Problem and Model Choice
sections.summary: The fundamental challenge is that chess engines cannot explain and LLMs cannot play well; the solution combines both. Gemini 2.5 Pro is identified as the best current chess model with visible reasoning improvements.

sections.title: Agent Tools Overview
sections.summary: The agent has tools for legal moves, a virtual chessboard for variation exploration, a chess engine, checks-captures-threats data, and web search for historical context.

sections.title: Checks-Captures-Threats Tool Deep Dive
sections.summary: The checks-captures-threats tool surfaces beginner-relevant candidate moves alongside the best move, providing diversity for the agent to explain human-reasonable moves and bad moves, not just engine-optimal play. A complicated position is shown where the best move is a rook sacrifice on E3.

sections.title: Who Should Do the Thinking
sections.summary: The project evolved from Python-scripted analysis to reasoning-model-driven analysis. Grok 4 was previously best; now Gemini 2.5 Pro is preferred. Conflicting tool-provided information is beneficial for balanced descriptions.

sections.title: Video Production and Channel Results
sections.summary: ElevenLabs V3 is used for TTS with emotional audio tags. The agent decides highlights, arrows, and brilliant-move labels. The channel has roughly 500k views and over 4,000 subscribers, not yet monetized.

sections.title: Q&A on Costs, Quality, and Error Rate
sections.summary: Not monetized yet, operating at a net loss. Automation was enabled recently; speaker still reviews manually at that point. Error rate is roughly 1 in 20 videos with issues like missed checkmates, providing debugging signal.

sections.title: Q&A on Cost per Video and Optimization
sections.summary: Average cost per video is 20-30 cents for short videos, but can reach euros for longer content. Cost optimization is deprioritized in favor of description quality. Optimization opportunities exist such as eliminating redundant tool calls where the agent replays a game twice. The speaker has shifted to a more relaxed approach, willing to remove bad videos afterwards rather than manual pre-review.

sections.title: Q&A on Human Move Simulation and Audience Targeting
sections.summary: The Maya engine from the University of Toronto can simulate moves at a given player rating, potentially enabling content targeted by skill level. There is ongoing uncertainty about which difficulty to target — some checkmate-in-one puzzles are trivial for strong players but valuable for absolute beginners. No other games have been explored yet, though extension is considered possible.
